findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Reconsider adopting flock(1) for the re-clone lock in THIS change (modeled on autodeploy.sh `exec 9>"$LOCK"; flock -n 9`) instead of the bespoke hard-linked-timestamp lock, since flock auto-releases on holder death — eliminating the STALE/WAIT/POLL knobs and the abandoned/unreadable/unremovable-lock ACs — and the deferral rationale ('re-plumbing tested code') does not apply to net-new, previously-untested lock code.
evidence: Plan: 'flock ... auto-releases on holder death and would make staleness moot; it is the better primitive, recorded as follow-up beton-inversive-stag rather than re-plumbing tested code inside a bug fix.'

Plan: 'Lock is ${REBAR_TRACKER_DIR}.reclone.lock, a regular file containing epoch seconds ... ln-ed into place ... MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_STALE=7200s and MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_WAIT=7200s ... Poll MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_POLL=10s.'
Repo prior art confirmed: infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh:436-437 `exec 9>"$LOCK"; flock -n 9 || { ...; exit 0; }` — same infra tree.
The lock is net-new code; the plan states the entrypoint clone path had 'the only possible test ... a grep over Dockerfile source', so no tested lock code exists to 're-plumb'.

Extra ACs exist purely to cover bespoke-lock failure modes flock avoids: 'An unreadable lock marker is treated as abandoned', 'An unremovable stale lock exhausts the wait budget', 'A container dying while holding the lock does not wedge the store.'
findings.finding: For the re-clone serialization (scope-growth item 2), the plan builds a bespoke hard-linked-timestamp lock (with STALE/WAIT/POLL knobs, staleness detection, unreadable-marker and unremovable-lock handling) while itself naming flock(1) as 'the better primitive' that 'would make staleness moot' and citing in-repo prior art — then defers flock on a rationale ('rather than re-plumbing tested code inside a bug fix') that does not apply, since the lock is entirely new code and the entrypoint path was untested. flock is a clearly-superior, available alternative that eliminates the very failure classes (abandoned/unreadable/unremovable lock) the plan must otherwise add extra ACs and tests to defend.
findings.location: Scope growth during implementation -> 2. Serialize the re-clone (Protocol / Alternatives weighed)
scenarios: A container dies mid-clone holding the file lock: flock releases automatically; the bespoke lock relies on a 7200s staleness heuristic before another container can proceed.
An unreadable/unremovable marker: flock has no marker to read; the bespoke design needs dedicated handling and tests.
findings.suggested_fix: Serialize the re-clone with a shell flock on a dedicated fd/lockfile (e.g. `exec 9>"${REBAR_TRACKER_DIR}.reclone.lock"; flock -w "$MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_WAIT" 9 || return 1`), then re-check `git -C "$DIR" rev-parse --verify -q HEAD` after acquiring so a peer's completed clone is observed without re-cloning. This preserves the loser-blocks-not-skips and peer-observes-completed-clone semantics while dropping the staleness/unreadable-marker/unremovable-lock machinery and their ACs.

Confirmed prior art: infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh:437 `flock -n 9 || { ... exit 0; }`; src/rebar/_snapshot/git_fetch.py:71 `interprocess_lock` is a reusable fcntl.flock(LOCK_EX)-with-mkdir-fallback contextmanager already covering the multi-process case

Plan invents new machinery (MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_STALE=7200, MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_WAIT=7200, MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_POLL=10, epoch-marker hardlink, stale reclaim, unreadable-marker-as-abandoned) whose entire purpose is to approximate the crash-safety flock gives for free

The 'tested code' rationale is weakened because scope growth §1 already moves the entrypoint into infra/scripts/mcp-entrypoint.sh as a fresh COPYed script, so a flock leg would not require re-plumbing existing tested Python
findings.finding: The plan builds a novel hand-rolled cross-process lock (hard-linked timestamp marker + MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_STALE/WAIT/POLL, staleness reclamation, unreadable-marker handling) while conceding in 'Alternatives weighed' that flock 'is the better primitive' that 'would make staleness moot' — reimplementing auto-release-on-death and stale-reclaim that flock/interprocess_lock provide for free; the anti-repackaging justification ('rather than re-plumbing tested code inside a bug fix') is undercut by the fact that scope growth already extracts the entrypoint into a new script and writes an entire new lock protocol from scratch.

scenarios: A container dies holding the bespoke lock: the plan needs the stale-reclaim + unreadable-marker + wait-budget logic (and its ACs) precisely to recover; flock -n on FD would auto-release with none of it
A future maintainer must reason about three new tuned timeouts and marker-atomicity, versus reusing one audited primitive

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Justify building a bespoke hard-linked-timestamp lock with three new config knobs (MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_STALE/_WAIT/_POLL) now, versus adopting the repo's existing cross-process lock idiom (fcntl.flock via _snapshot.git_fetch.interprocess_lock, or shell `flock -n` as in autodeploy.sh:437) which auto-releases on holder death and eliminates the staleness/abandoned-lock/unreadable-marker machinery (and its ~5 ACs) the plan concedes flock would make moot.
evidence: Plan quote: 'flock (repo prior art: autodeploy.sh flock -n 9, _snapshot/git_fetch.interprocess_lock) auto-releases on holder death and would make staleness moot; it is the better primitive'

Existing primitive: src/rebar/_snapshot/git_fetch.py:71 interprocess_lock (fcntl.flock(LOCK_EX) + mkdir fallback), called at src/rebar/_snapshot/cache.py:119,257; and flock -n 9 in the SAME infra tree at infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh:437
Config proliferation: three new env knobs MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_STALE=7200/_WAIT=7200/_POLL=10 introduced solely to service the bespoke lock's manual staleness logic

Five of the eight additional ACs (abandoned-lock broken, unreadable-timestamp treated as abandoned, unremovable-stale exhausts budget, concurrent-reclone not interleaved, peer-finishing-clone) exist only to cover staleness machinery that a kernel-auto-released flock would not need
findings.finding: The plan hand-rolls a bespoke hard-linked-timestamp cross-process lock with three new config knobs (MCP_RECLONE_LOCK_STALE/_WAIT/_POLL) while the codebase already standardizes on a reusable cross-process lock primitive, and the plan itself concedes flock is the better primitive that would make the staleness machinery moot.
findings.location: Scope growth during implementation section 2 ('Serialize the re-clone' -> 'Protocol' and 'Alternatives weighed')
scenarios: A container dies holding the bespoke lock: the plan relies on a 7200s staleness timeout to break it, whereas flock releases immediately on process death
A future maintainer must reason about STALE vs WAIT budgets and unreadable-marker semantics instead of reusing the one lock idiom already in the repo
findings.suggested_fix: Either (a) use `flock` (shell `flock -n <fd>` on ${REBAR_TRACKER_DIR}.reclone.lock, testable via the existing autodeploy flock-stub pattern in tests/scripts/) or a small shell wrapper over the same flock(2) semantics interprocess_lock uses, dropping the STALE/WAIT/POLL knobs and the abandoned/unreadable-marker ACs; or (b) if flock is genuinely unavailable in this container, state that constraint explicitly and scope the bespoke lock as the deliberate interim, rather than deferring the acknowledged-better primitive to beton-inversive-stag while shipping the reinvented one.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Distinguish transient rev-parse failures (index.lock / concurrent gc) from genuine poison before destructively clearing, so a healthy store under concurrent git maintenance is not wiped.
evidence: Plan: "Require a RESOLVABLE HEAD before trusting the clone, and clear the directory before re-cloning"
Plan states healthy stores resolve HEAD, but does not rule out transient rev-parse failures on a healthy store (concurrent git maintenance, index.lock) that would trip the destructive clear
The clear is irreversible on a persistent named volume and there is no flag/dry-run gating the destructive branch
findings.finding: The gate treats any non-resolvable HEAD as poison and destructively clears the persistent volume, but does not distinguish a genuinely-poisoned store from a HEALTHY store whose HEAD is transiently unresolvable — e.g. a concurrent `git gc`/`index.lock`, a repack in progress, or an in-flight fetch on the same volume could make `rev-parse --verify HEAD` fail momentarily, causing an irreversible `clear_tracker_dir` of a good ~1.9G store.
scenarios: A healthy store undergoing concurrent git maintenance (gc/repack) or holding a stale index.lock returns non-zero from rev-parse; the new gate then clears the good store and forces a needless ~200k-commit re-clone, and if the clone then fails (offline/PAT expiry) the store is left empty
findings.suggested_fix: Before clearing, confirm the directory is genuinely unusable (e.g. also require that a bounded retry after removing a stale index.lock still fails, or gate the destructive clear on an explicit non-transient signal) rather than clearing on the first non-zero rev-parse.
